science.title: What cannot be taught: the apprenticeship problem in modern Chinese medicine
science.description: Apprenticeship has long served as the primary mode of transmission in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), cultivating clinical judgment learned less through explicit instruction than through shared experience, observation, and the gradual internalization of a master’s diagnostic sensibilities. Yet the twentieth-century shift toward university-based standardization—mirroring global movements of professionalization—reshaped the epistemic foundations of the field. What apprenticeship once safeguarded as tacit, contextual, and adaptive was increasingly reframed as insufficiently measurable, reproducible, or legitimate. As TCM entered institutional systems in China, North America, Australia, and Europe, a central tension emerged: modern training structures excel at teaching what can be codified but struggle to preserve forms of expertise that cannot. Using the Pu–Wang lineage as an analytic lens, this paper examines how experiential mastery and formula systematization represent contrasting responses to this tension. Pu Fuzhou’s clinical practice exemplified an apprenticeship-based epistemology grounded in intuition and case-specific reasoning, while Wang Mianzhi translated elements of this sensibility into a framework more compatible with academic instruction. Their intertwined trajectories illuminate a broader dilemma surrounding the modernization of traditional medical systems: how to institutionalize a practice whose core strengths lie in forms of knowledge that resist formalization. Drawing on historical sources, comparative education studies, and cross-national regulatory analysis, the paper argues that the apprenticeship problem in modern TCM is not merely pedagogical but epistemic. It reflects competing understandings of valid knowledge, the cultivation of clinical authority, and the forms of reasoning that should define the modern practitioner. The study proposes a hybrid approach that preserves the tacit dimensions of apprenticeship while meeting contemporary demands for standardization and professional recognition. In doing so, it contributes a conceptual framework for rethinking the future of TCM education and offers broader insights into the preservation and transmission of experiential knowledge in professional training systems.

science.title: Odorant receptor coexpression and multi-expression in the dengue mosquito
science.description: Drosophila olfactory sensory neurons tend to express a single ligand-specific receptor, following a one-receptor-per-neuron rule expected to apply broadly across insects. Recent work challenges this view by showing that some neurons in the mosquito Aedes aegypti coexpress multiple receptors. However, the full extent and nature of coexpression in Ae. aegypti remains unclear. We sequenced the transcriptomes of 46,000 female antennal neurons to resolve all olfactory neuron subtypes and identify expressed receptors. Half of all subtypes coexpress multiple receptors. However, coexpression occurs almost exclusively among receptors from the same family; cross-family coexpression of odorant receptors with ionotropic receptors is rare. We also document a phenomenon called multi-expression, wherein one receptor is expressed in multiple neuron subtypes, often alongside distant paralogs. Drosophila provides rare examples of both coexpression and multi-expression, suggesting that Drosophila and Aedes are not fundamentally different, but instead located at different positions along a continuum likely to encompass diverse insects. Dengue mosquito olfactory neurons are known to show complex patterns of receptor expression, but the details of this complexity remain unclear. Here, the authors build a comprehensive molecular atlas of antennal neurons, showing that half express multiple receptors and that some receptors are expressed in multiple neurons.

science.title: Neptune's tiny moons tell the story of Triton's destructive capture
science.description: Neptune's moon and ring system stand out among the giant planets because of the strange imbalance between its one very large moon and its many tiny moons. Its largest moon, Triton, makes up more than 99% of the mass of all satellites orbiting the planet while orbiting retrograde compared with Neptune's rotation. The predominant theory is that Triton is a captured Kuiper Belt object that caused a major disruption in Neptune's early moon system. Now, a new study published in Science Advances provides spectroscopic evidence to support this theory.
